title: State Applied Before Its Write-Ahead Log Record Is Durable
pattern: Code that maintains a log for durability or recovery applies a change to in-memory state or to on-disk data pages before the corresponding log record has been appended and synced.
why_bad: The write-ahead invariant is that the log is the source of truth: nothing may reflect a change the log does not yet durably contain. If the log append fails, memory reports a state that will vanish on restart and may already have been served to readers. If the process crashes after a page write but before the WAL sync, recovery cannot redo or undo the change, leaving torn or unrecoverable pages.
detection: In a storage engine, state machine, or persistence layer: a mutation of the in-memory structure (`insert`, `push`, field assignment) or a data-file write/flush that precedes, on the same path, the append and `sync_all`/`sync_data`/`fsync` of the log record describing that change; or an error path after the log write fails that does not revert the already-applied state.
counterexample: Log-then-apply ordering (append, fsync, then mutate memory or write pages); steal/no-force buffer managers whose page flushes are gated on the page LSN being durable in the WAL; purely volatile caches with no durability claim.
source: Alex Petrov, *Database Internals* (2019), Ch. 5, p. 83; Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* (2017), Ch. 3, p. 80; Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance* (2013), Ch. 13, p. 632.
